provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held due process does not categorically require appointed counsel for an indigent parent in every termination proceeding, leaving the question to case-by-case determination by the trial court subject to appellate review.
key_cases.relevance: Sets the federal due process floor for appointed counsel in termination cases; Oregon exceeds it by statute in ORS 419B.205, which is why Oregon litigation turns on the adequacy rather than the existence of counsel.
key_cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that due process requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before terminating parental rights, invalidating New York's preponderance standard.
key_cases.relevance: This is the federal constitutional floor that Oregon's ORS 419B.521 clear-and-convincing standard implements, and the authority a parent invokes if any lesser standard is applied.
key_cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel Dept. of Human Services v. Rardin
key_cases.holding: Reversing a termination judgment, the court held that because ORS 419B.504 permits termination only on grounds of present unfitness, the statute assumes parents can change, and a father whose earlier conduct had changed genuinely and lastingly could not be found unfit for failing to present an agency-satisfactory reintegration plan.
key_cases.relevance: Completes the Stillman–Simmons line by holding that genuine and lasting change in a parent's conduct forecloses termination for unfitness, because ORS 419B.504 reaches only present unfitness.
key_cases.quote: the legislature assumes that parents can change their conduct and that, if the change is both genuine and lasting, the state may not terminate their parental rights for unfitness

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel SOSCF v. Stillman
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed reversal of termination, construing ORS 419B.504 to require a two-part showing — present unfitness from seriously detrimental conduct or condition, and improbability of integration within a reasonable time — and holding an incarcerated father's drug history did not make him presently unfit.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading Oregon Supreme Court construction of the ORS 419B.504 unfitness ground, and the source of the two-part test every later Oregon termination case applies.
key_cases.quote: ORS 419B.504 sets out a two-part test for determining whether to terminate parental rights, both parts of which must be met before the court orders termination.

key_cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. T. M. D.
key_cases.holding: The court held there is no statutory presumption or preference favoring termination over permanent guardianship, that the department bears the full burden on best interests, and on this record termination was not in the child's best interest.
key_cases.relevance: Controls the best-interests half of an Oregon termination case and rejects any thumb on the scale in favor of adoption over less drastic permanency.
key_cases.quote: The department must prove only that that the parent's conduct justifies termination and that the best interest of the child will be served by termination.

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel Dept. of Human Services v. Simmons
key_cases.holding: Reversing termination, the court held the State had not proved by clear and convincing evidence that mother's mental illness and past substance addiction made her unfit at the time of the termination trial, the only time frame that matters.
key_cases.relevance: Sets the Oregon Supreme Court's controlling application of the clear-and-convincing unfitness standard, measured at the time of the termination trial rather than on historical conduct.
key_cases.quote: On this record, there is not clear and convincing evidence of a present drug abuse problem that would render mother unfit at the time of the termination trial.

key_cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. M. A. N.
key_cases.holding: On de novo review in an ICWA case, the court held mother was unfit but that the State failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that termination was in the child's best interest where he was placed long-term with bonded extended family, and reversed.
key_cases.relevance: Shows that in an ICWA case the best-interests element must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt, not merely by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.quote: DHS has failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that termination of mother's parental rights is in his best interest
